utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted, Tom Hannis, and Crispian Smith, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Ms. Melody Whittaker, appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic, appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't know if there are any housekeeping mattering that counsel have before the witness is recalled to the stand, but from the Chamber -- from the Bench's point of view picking up from where we left on Friday as to the -- what's going happen the rest of this week. I think counsel for the OTP had raised the possibility of sitting on Friday to complete the witnesses that they had scheduled, but having regard to the -- Friday, the 19th having been previously fixed as a dies non juridicus, it is from the Chamber's point of view impossible to reverse that. So counsel should bear in mind that we have available today and tomorrow, and in terms of the OTP's schedule of witnesses, and we alerted before we took the bench, that the continued examination-in-chief of the witness who is now on the stand is likely to occupy the whole of today. Counsel for the OTP would -- should advise themselves accordingly and so adjust their witnesses list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir. Before Mr. Olmsted resumes his examination-in-chief of you, I remind you you're still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sejmenovic.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to begin today by clarifying just a few matters that were -- that we questioned you about last Friday. First of all, last Friday when I asked you whether the non-Serb population in Prijedor was attempting to obtain weapons prior to the takeover, you told us that some people strove to come by weapons for their personal safety but this was done in an uninstitutional manner. Can you clarify for us what you meant by "uninstitutional manner"?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I answer the question, I would like to note that I still owe you the last answer before the recess we had, and the question was that I should briefly describe the atmosphere that reigned in the days preceding the takeover, so if I may in a couple of sentences, I would like do that. I think it would be helpful to all in the courtroom to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I think it would. Let me clarify this particular matter and then we can move right to that because that's actually within the area of my next questions for you. So just to -- focussing on this pre-takeover period, what you meant by uninstitutional manner, which some non-Serbs were obtaining arms?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The atmosphere I'm referring to was such that the non-Serb population were in a highly insecure situation. Given that, and in view of the fact that they saw that the official authorities did nothing to remedy the situation, they tried to protect themselves. They were left to their own devices. We knew that the army was arming the Serbian population. The non-Serb population of whatever ethnicity was not receiving weapons from anyone. Under the circumstances, some individuals tried to obtain weapons or purchase weapons for themselves either through arms smell smuggling or from members of the reserve force. We did not have any reliable information on this, however. Those were only assumptions that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were these persons, these non-Serb persons who were seeking to obtain arms, were they getting them from Serbs in the area?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard information to the effect that certain individuals had purchased weapons from Serbs, members of the reserve force, or soldiers who returned home and that they were able to purchase weapons from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us what kinds of weapons they were able to obtain through these means?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt this information as unverified, and it wasn't from first knowledge -- first-hand knowledge. Apparently, a lad from Omarska sold weapons to a lad in Kozarac. I heard stores to the effect that this young man was able to buy weapons from the Serbs in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, my question is: What kind of arms? Were these any kind of heavy arms or weapons, any artillery or were these just basic weapons?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I remember, it was an automatic rifle that was the case in this instance -- situation, or semi-automatic; I'm not sure anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. Now I want to move to the atmosphere prior to the takeover. Did you want to supplement what you had told us yesterday? Or on Friday, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I wanted to answer the question but we had to adjourn so I was unable to. It may be helpful to the Chamber. I'm referring to the month of April, i.e., the period preceding the takeover. At the time, Serb forces would appear in Prijedor in several formations. Prijedor was milling with reservist, members of the 5th Kozara Brigade. It was through the Prijedor and the villages surrounding Prijedor that regular soldiers of the JNA would pass. One could also see members of the Matic's police in Prijedor from the neighbouring Croatia or, rather, the Serbian Krajina, SRK. At the time, a war was waged in Croatia where in these autonomous provinces independence was claimed. There had already been casualties in several towns. And the scenario was always the same. The army or the police would barge in and cause a massacre. I remember one in Bijeljina, in Zvornik, and I think there was another one in Brcko as well. Around Prijedor, the SDS had taken power in most of the municipalities around Prijedor, a coup was carried out in Sanski Most, they took over power, and a neighbourhood in Sanski Most was torched by artillery fire. This was the pervasive atmosphere in mid-April 1992. At the same time, the Republican Staff of Territorial Defence issued an order that the country should be defended and that the population should be defended. At the municipal level in Prijedor, we were unable to carry out the order because the structures arriving from the SDS stone walled and obstructed these efforts. In mid-April, reenforcements arrived to all the various forces I mentioned around Prijedor and around non-Serb territories. We were still operating within institutions but were unable to exercise in the territory of Prijedor municipality and implement the orders arriving from the republican level. There was a possibility for some initiative at the local level and there was also the pressure brought to bear upon us because of the general situation that existed in the area, pressure from the population. There were also tensions where -- in the areas where Serb populated areas bordered with non-Serb populated ones. I also said that overnight certain white flags or markings would be placed on houses and these were Serb houses in -- on -- in the outlying but -- areas close to the boundary. All this pointed to the fact that the Serbs wanted to engage in actions. If you went through a village which was a non-Serb village, pure non-Serb village, during the night, you would see people take -- standing guard in front of their houses. So there wasn't a system in place. What they were attempting to do was to comply with the instructions from the republican authorities, and the municipality was supposed to take care of the population's security and to take measures and precautions to possibly protect the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm sorry for the intervention in the transcript, 6, line 6; page 6, line 6, I believe the -- the witness mentioned Territorial Defence and it was recorded as municipality. Perhaps municipality Territorial Defence. Maybe you clarify that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Territorial Defence at the level of the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Last Friday one of the things that you mentioned that you observed in the days leading up to the takeover of the municipality was that women, children, and elderly left their homes during the night and only returned in the morning. What were the ethnicities of these people who would leave during the night?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were solely Serbs from the Serb villages bordering with non-Serb villages. The Serbian population was leaving and they would be mostly the elderly, women, and children. They would leave their homes during the night and then come back in the morning. And, of course, people would inquire of them in the morning as to what had happened the previous night. But they would always deny everything. They would say, No, we didn't leave. You are must have -- you must be mistaken, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you explain to us why this phenomenon of people leaving during the night and coming back the next morning was related -- or how you perceive it as being related to the eventually takeover of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time before the takeover, as these things were happening, we were quite clear on the fact that the army was getting ready for actions and that that was the reason why they were pulling the Serbian population out of the area, in order to enable them to carry out their actions. And it was only logical to conclude this. However, in the mornings, nothing would really happen. People would come back to their homes, and this is what would happen, once, twice, and we realised that these must have been drills in the event of an actual attack that they should be ready. There were no indications. There wasn't a single reason for any Serbian village to be evacuated in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You testified last Friday that you heard public announcements that the non-Serbs were getting ready to attack Prijedor and this was even published in an Official Gazette. Who issued these announcements?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the SDS that published it, or, rather, the public controlling the SDS. It was a component part of a campaign that had long been in the making and been implemented. The SDS created an atmosphere of fear among the Serbian population through their representatives. The SDS took control of all the TV installations in the area, and broadcast its own programme solely, the news from the battle-field in Croatia, the news from Belgrade, their own newscasts, and the news programme was designed deliberately with a view to promoting or implementing a political propaganda which wanted to instill fear with the Serbian population and to simply carry out a propaganda among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to be clear, were there any plans by the non-Serbs to attack either Prijedor town or any part of the municipality at any time prior to the takeover of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, at no point in time from anyone person, either civilian or a member of the Territorial Defence, did I ever hear or -- of or see any sort of plan, any mention of it or even any mention of a possibility for a Serbian area or a Serbian home or a Serbian individual to be attacked. The SDA policy, as well as that of all the other parties outside of the Serbian block, outside of the SDS, was to do all in one's power to dispel such unfounded fears. Various peace initiatives were launched, such as ones to set up joint movements, civic fora, joint patrol, mixed military formations which would be composed of the army from the 5th Kozara Brigade, the police, the Territorial Defence in Kozarac, and wherever the army and the SDS agreed, such mixed army units would be set up. But the Serbs refused all of it. Individuals of Serb ethnicity who were committed to peace and civilised life were at risk from the SDS and slowly moved out or withdrew from such civic associations or organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did either the SDS or HDZ leadership in Prijedor receive any instructions from their republican Main Boards to establish Crisis Staffs in Prijedor or separate government institutions?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDS did receive such orders, because it had already established a parallel state by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it was a slip of my tongue. The SDA or the HDZ, did the non-Serb political parties receive any such instructions from their Main Boards.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They had not received any instructions about divisions. The SDA and the HDZ and many of the civic parties of the opposition were operating at the time and had an intention to operate within the bounds of the law, the constitution and institutions that were legitimately elected. What the SDA or non-Serb politicians weren't able to carry out were some of the orders arriving from the state level. They were unable to prevent the SDS from cutting off the financial ties between Prijedor and the rest of the state, because the functionary within the SDK was one who co-operated with the SDS and syphoned off the financial -- the flow of payments from -- from Sarajevo to Banja Luka, to the autonomous province that had, by that time, already been set up there. The mobilisation of territorial staff -- Defence, that is, could also not be carried out although we had received an order from the republican level to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In fact, that was my next question. Prior to the takeover, had the TO units in the non-Serb areas of Prijedor been mobilised? And I believe that you have just answered that they could not have been -- you were unable to carry out any instructions to that regard.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they could not have been mobilised because the centre for mobilisation, that is to say the main command in the municipality was in the city of Prijedor. Of course, in that command there were people from the SDS as well, and the order to mobilise the Territorial Defence could not have been implemented in the way it should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to move now to the takeover itself. Did you go to Prijedor town on the morning after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went to Prijedor that morning normally to the meeting that had been agreed, not knowing that what is going on, and at the first stop of the bus, when army troops came onto the bus starting to check papers of the passengers, I realised something out of the ordinary was happening and I saw at the bus-stop sandbags and machine-gun emplacement. The soldiers were checking the IDs of the passengers on the bus. They looked at my ID and returned it to me without a word. They didn't say anything to me or to the other passengers. The bus continued on to Prijedor, and at all the following major intersections we could see soldiers and machine-gun emplacements. And just before the main bus terminal, the railway station at the main intersection in Prijedor near the SUP building outside the town hall, it was the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did you also see police guarding these facilities?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was a mixed composition. There were soldiers, police, and military police. Military police wore military uniforms with white belts. So it was a mixed force that carried out this takeover, this military putsch.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now when arrived in town, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived in town, I went, first, to the party headquarters, because that's where I had planned to go, and there I found some members of the party standing outside. They were trying to get in, but they couldn't because the lock had been changed. A cleaning lady came out and told us, There's nothing for us to do there. She would call the police if we continued trying to get in, so we left, and we set out towards the municipality building. There were non-Serbs standing outside, employees of the municipality who had worked there as recently as the day before but were unable to get in, were not allowed, and the president of the municipality, Muhamed Cehajic, was there. He was also standing at the reception desk not being allowed to get in.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us, at this point in time who were the main SDA leaders in Prijedor? Obviously we don't want a complete list, but if could you just give us the main SDA leaders.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean SDS or SDA?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: SDA.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well the president was Mirzad Mujadzic, vice-president; Camil Pezo; then myself. I can't remember the third vice-president. The Executive Board included Sefer Krkic, Ilijaz Music, Muhamed Cehajic, Becir Mehdunjanin, Ilijaz Memic, I believe was also on the Executive Board. Rufad Suljanovic, Dr. Rufad Suljanovic was also on the Executive Board. I could actually give you all the names, if given a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine. That will do. Were members of the SDA leadership who held government positions allowed to return to their positions, their jobs in the weeks or months that followed the takeover?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one at no time, although they tried to make inquiries by telephone, none of them were allowed to return. What happened the next day, happened in companies and enterprises. Managers of non-Serb ethnicity were refused access to their workplaces. Senior staff in public -- publicly owned companies were also refused access to their workplaces and even ordinary workers were not allowed to go back to work. In some enterprises they were exceptions, I know, for instance, about the service in charge of railway maintenance. There was a non-Serb or a few non-Serbs who were allowed to go on working. As for banks and major companies, major businesses, all non-Serbs who had occupied posts of any importance were refused access and Serbs took over their works -- the workplaces.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, it wasn't simply members of the SDA who were denied the opportunity to return to their jobs, it was all non-Serbs except for the exceptions that you gave?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened to the members of the SDA leadership in the aftermath of the takeover?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the takeover, the SDA leadership never managed to convene again in full composition. There were one or two attempts but they were never able to meet again, all of them. The first thing we did was approach SDS, suggesting that we talk about the situation and discuss the moves they had made.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I want to move on to that in a second. Did the members of the SDA leadership, did they survive the conflict, did they survive 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three men survived from the leadership. And 90 to 95 per cent of municipal and local officials were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What happened to the non-Serb police officers in Prijedor, after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, policemen turned up for work. Some were turned back without any explanation, but I heard that some others were offered a statement of loyalty to sign. I'm not aware that anyone actually signed it. In fact, I heard that some did but I didn't know these men. But it's quite certain that within a few days even those who were prepared to sign that statement, were no longer working in the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at 65 ter 2418. This is tab number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This a decision on the termination of employment. It's dated 16 October 1992. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And without going into any details, who showed it to you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received that document from the man who is named here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: As the reason for the decision, it states that the Prijedor Crisis Staff ordered all work organisations to terminate the employment of all employee who is had participated in the armed rebellion around are currently in one of the refugee camps, Omarska or Keraterm. Did you spend any time in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Would you classify it as a refugee camp?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. It was a concentration camp by any standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were only non-Serbs detained at Omarska and Keraterm fired from their jobs in state-owned enterprises?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Everyone was fired, regardless of whether they had been in Omarska or Keraterm, even women were laid off. Dismissals from work had nothing to do with Keraterm and Omarska, and that started happening even before these camps were established.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01715, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I now want to move to events after the takeover.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were any travel restrictions imposed on the non-Serb population in Prijedor municipality, after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's not that restrictions were imposed but travel was no longer possible. It was prohibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Where were you living -- or where were you spending most of your time after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Trnopolje, in my birth place, my place of residence, and I went occasionally to Kozarac and came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Other than travelling to Kozarac and that area, the non-Serb area around Kozarac, were you able to travel around the municipality freely; for instance, going into Prijedor town or other locations?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not freely. Free travel was possible just the first few days after the takeover. Later on, it was no longer possible because public transport was cancelled and it was based in Prijedor, so there was no more public transport. And travelling in your own car meant that you would be stopped and your papers would be checked at several check-points, and we had also heard that some people had been stopped at these check-points, their cars taken away, and they had to walk back home. That meant practically that it was a total blockade. Several days after the takeover, you were not able to go to Prijedor by any means at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who was manning these check-points?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police and reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And during this time-period, did you hear about any crimes committed against non-Serbs at these check-points?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were cases at the check-point on the way to Omarska. People were beaten up, their cars taken away. There was also an incident at the entry point to Prijedor, but I don't know the details. The person was probably beaten up as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And during this period between the takeover and the attack on Kozarac, were non-Serbs in Kozarac allowed to move out of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Does that include women, children, and elderly?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That includes everyone. Some people tried, but women and children were turned back.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did you ever seek an explanation for why they weren't allowed to leave the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they stopped people going to Banja Luka the first time, we still had some communication from them. The official explanation was the one that could be heard even earlier in the form of propaganda. Namely, that we were preparing to go to war against Serbs and that we were trying to send our women and children away from Prijedor municipality. However, at the same time, we could see that Serb women and children were being allowed to leave Prijedor. However, no discussion was possible. Their accusations were final. What used to be propaganda turned into an official position that was later published in newspapers and other media.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were non-Serb children allowed to attend school after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, secondary schools were based only in Prijedor. From the moment the road from Prijedor to Kozarac was blocked and when there was no more public transport available, non-Serb children from Kozarac were no longer able to attend secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What happened to the electricity and telephone service in Kozarac after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the takeover, we continued to have electricity and telephone service for a while and then both were cut off. Several days before the attack, they cut off both.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you explain to us how you know that it was cut off as opposed to simply malfunctioning?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kozarac had no electricity. Kamicani and Jakupovici did not have electricity either, all those settlements. However, Petrov Gaj and Omarska and Serb hamlets adjacent to Trnopolje had electricity. If I can remember well, there were two non-Serb houses on the boundary that had electricity and one of the houses had a working telephone. All the rest had no power and no telephone. Now, looking towards the west, across from Ribnjak and Tomasica village, they had electricity throughout, the town of Prijedor as well. You could see that very clearly every evening, every night.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's bring up 65 ter 10580. This is tab 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And while we're bringing that up, what JNA unit did you serve in during your compulsory military service after secondary school?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in an artillery unit. It was a 105-millimetre Howitzer unit; that's how we called it. We called it Howitzer 105. Those were medium-calibre guns, you can call them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can zoom in just a little bit more. And then scroll -- oh, not that much. That's too much as well. Just a little bit, not ... and if we could actually scroll up towards the top. There you go. There you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, in the first half of May, was any artillery positioned around Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was artillery even in April, before the takeover at certain positions around Kozarac. As best I can remember, I'll explain where they were. The guns were here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Wait, let's --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cannons were here --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. Let's skip the image right and then, yes, I would like you to mark with an X where you saw various artillery positions around Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Artillery positions were here. And somewhere here too. Then in this area. A position also at Benkovac overlooking Kozarac, I can't see Benkovac. Here, I think. And then in the area of the quarry and the mine there were some positions, in Orlovci, somewhere here. At the airport at Urije, I suppose it's here. Around here. I'm not quite sure. Again, at Gornja Puharska, it's either here or here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who -- who put this artillery at these various locations around Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, officially, there was the Yugoslavia People's Army, the Yugoslav army, although members of the 5th Kozara Brigade were seen there. People who were coming back from the theatre of war in Croatia returning to their homes were observed in some of these locations after their return.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you describe for us the kinds of artillery that were positioned around Kozarac. You mentioned you were with a Howitzer unit in a JNA. Were any of those placed around Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even before these incidents we knew that multi-barrel rocket-launchers were at the Urije airport. Large-calibre cannons were in Urije and in Gornja Puharska. There was artillery in Gorazde. At Benkovci there were regular Yugoslavia army troops and they had several large-calibre batteries. We knew that as well. At the quarry, we supposed there were some because soldiers had been seen hauling something and setting something up. And later when they started to use the artillery, we realised it was a smaller calibre. And when the attack happened, those who had seen artillery fire while serving in the army were aware what it looked like when shells were fired from Howitzers of 155 millimetres, the devastation is huge. And with these guns you can hear both the explosion and later, 15, 20 seconds later, depending on the distance, you can also hear the sounds of fire, the firing. Prijedor was shelled with heavy artillery from Benkovac and Omarska and that's it for the heavy artillery. With smaller-calibre artillery from Orlovic, Donji Gorazde and the quarry. The artillery from Tomasica that I'm showing near this fish pond was never used. It fired only twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we're going into in the attack on Kozarac in a little bit. I did have one clarification for your last answer. You said Prijedor was shelled with heavy artillery. Did you mean Prijedor or were you referring to Kozarac area?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I was speaking too fast for interpreters. Kozarac was shelled with heavy artillery from Prijedor, from the area of Urije or Gornja Puharska. So, the shells were coming from this direction, this direction, and this direction. That's heavy artillery. And lighter artillery and mortars were firing from this direction and this direction and somewhere from this area which I did not mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I want to talk about this period of April and early May, when these artillery positions were established around Kozarac. Were you able to observe in which directions these weapons were faced?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not go to any of these places. We knew that because we heard from people who had been there and told us, either people from the party or the municipal structures. We knew some of the reservists who were part of these units, and when they deserted, they told us about it. They told us of the positions. Also, villagers from neighbouring villages saw these positions and told us from the municipality. But when the shelling began, I'll mark the position where I was when the shelling began.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just for the record, he just drew a circle as to where he was when the shelling began.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me focus you on my question though. You've now mentioned these artillery positions were established in late April -- in April and early May. Were you able to determine in which direction, say, the Howitzers were facing? Were they facing away from Kozarac or towards it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were facing towards Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise for interrupting, but in his previous answer the witness said I personally didn't go to any of these locations. How can he then know which direction the guns were facing?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness can --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as responsible people, we were in constant contact with people who came and informed us either because they were afraid and wanted to have answers for what was happening. As for the artillery, everybody said that the artillery guns were facing Kozarac expect for one battery in Urije which wasn't facing in this direction. It was facing at an angle of 90 degrees in this direction, so sort of towards town.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I object to this document. What assistance does it have? The witness didn't see any of these locations, he didn't see whether there was any action from these locations, nor does very any personal knowledge. He said, I heard from some people, but he didn't say the source. And we don't see how this map could assist the Chamber. He doesn't have any knowledge of actions nor does he have personal knowledge. He is merely talking about something that heard from others. This is not even hearsay. It's -- who knows who he heard it from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me, Your Honours, I'm trying to economise with time so I may be speaking too quickly. We had a few reservists who left the 5th Kozara Brigade. There was a lieutenant or second lieutenant who had been at some of these locations and he told me us about what he saw there. He gave us some additional information which I didn't talk about because I wasn't asked. That's one of the things that I'm talking about. The second is that shells can't just fall out of the sky. They come from certain directions and they hit certain locations. And you know exactly whether the whistling sound is above your head or whether it is coming from the opposite direction. Those who had served in the army and had some training knew very well that it wasn't difficult to establish where artillery shells were coming from. Only very exceptional geographic circumstances is a -- difficult to establish when, for example you're in the hills and the sound reverberates, so it's difficult to orient yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think he --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And one other very important thing. We didn't get the information for any of these places from only one person. The head of the municipality and the party was visited by people on several occasions. Ten people had come from Gornja Puharska to complain about these guns. And I can't have any doubt if people come to complain every single day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It seems to me, Mr. Krgovic, that, if anything, the -- an argument could be made about weight, but I see no reason why the document shouldn't be admitted based on this witness's testimony. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01716, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, I think you mentioned this in response to one of my prior questions, but did you and the other members of the SDA leadership attempt to meet with the SDS leadership in Prijedor following the takeover?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. There was several attempts and several meetings were held. The police, after the takeover of power, called the police in Kozarac so I know there were some contacts there, and I know that a team from the police went to negotiate. I know that a delegation went to a meeting to Banja Luka to meet with Kupresanin and Zupljanin, and I know that another delegation went to the SUP in Prijedor to the police, one went to the barracks and this was more or less unsuccessful. The SDA tried, at the level of the SDS party which was in control of everything, to set up a meeting and we managed to convince the SDS to hold this meeting. The meeting was held in Prijedor and I was personally there at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm going ask you about that meeting, but before I do, you mentioned this meeting in Prijedor with Kupresanin and Zupljanin. Was that Stojan Zupljanin, the CSB chief at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, had this is the first time that the Prosecutor has mentioned this. We were not informed about this. The witness didn't talk about this at all, nor did the Prosecutor inform us about this. I would like this to be stricken from the record and not to be -- and I would like the Prosecutor not to be allowed to go along this line. This is not professional behaviour. The Prosecutor never informed us about this and they didn't supply with us a proofing note that would contain this information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Before you answer, sir, just a moment. Your Honours, this is the first I heard about this too and that's why it is not in any proofing notes but he has now given an answer. He's mentioned someone by the name of Zupljanin and I think it is now my right to ask him which Zupljanin it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have to see where this goes, the witness having volunteered that information. We will see where it goes because it may very well in result in counsel for Zupljanin being given time to deal with this in their cross-examination. But as I said, the witness has volunteered it, so let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us which Zupljanin you were referring to who attended this meeting with members of the Kozarac police?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It is misleading. The witness never mentioned a meeting in Kozarac. What is going with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No, I didn't say there was a meeting in Kozarac. I'm reading from the record. Let's let the witness then explain to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned there was a meeting in which Zupljanin and Kupresanin attended or participated in. First of all, can you tell us which Zupljanin you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the chief of police, that Zupljanin. If I can provide some details because some of the parties are contesting this. Let me explain how this meeting happened. Vojislav Kupresanin was the president of the autonomous region of Krajina and he had a brother. His brother's wife was Hamdo Balic's sister, who was from Kozarac. And along that personal line Hamdo Balic from Kozarac, the brother-in-law of Kupresanin, was asked for -- and told for Kupresanin to ask Zupljanin to meet with a delegation from Kozarac which would explain that we were not armed, that we had no bad intentions towards the Serbs, that they were prepared to solve issues together and then this delegation went to Banja Luka. Becir Mehdunjanin led the delegation, and I think Hamdo Balic was also there, who was Kupresanin's brother-in-law. In a way he was his brother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us approximately when this meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some time between the 15th and 20th of May, I think. It was the second part of May, not later than the 20th of May. I'm not completely sure. Another piece of information. Dusan Tadic from Kozarac was also supposed to be a member of this delegation, together with some other Serbs. Dusan Tadic is the person whose case was heard before this Tribunal. This delegation went to Banja Luka and had some talks but there were no positive results. The explanations provided by the delegation were not recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to move on to the meeting that you attended with other members of the SDA leadership with the SDS leadership. First of all, can you tell us when that meeting occurred?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That meeting occurred sometime in mid-May.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never sure of the exact date because lots of things were happening at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you explain to us why you and the other members of the SDA leadership wanted to have this meeting with the SDS leadership?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several reasons. First, we were under complete blockade. Normal life was completely interrupted. People were terribly afraid. They were locked up in that area. We were afraid of an attack. We were not preparing any sort of an attack. We didn't even have any defence prepared. We wanted to talk to the SDS about the situation. We wanted to offer some solutions out of this situation. Everything that the SDS mentioned as reasons for a military coup we wanted to convince them that these reasons didn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And where did this meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the premises of the SDS in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And other than yourself, who from the SDA leadership was present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there; Becir Medunjanin was there; Mustafa Tadzic, from Kozarac; Islam Bahonjic; Professor Ilijaz Music; Meho Tursic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Who from the SDS leadership was present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On behalf of the SDS, it was President Simo Miskovic; Dragan or Dusan Kurnoga; Slobodan Kuruzovic; some security officials from military security and also from public security; Commander Arsic, he was a lieutenant-colonel, or colonel; and Major Zeljaja, who was the garrison commander in Prijedor and Arsic was the commander of the 5th Kozara --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you now tell us briefly what happened at this meeting with the SDS leadership and representatives from the military and public security?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After a few jokes made by the SDS and the officers, I must tell you first that Simo Miskovic, the president of the SDS, refused to start the meeting until the officers were there, and the meeting started only after the officers had arrived. Professor Music spoke first, I believe. He talked about the difficult situation. He said that people needed to be reinstated in their jobs, something to that effect. However, then the officers took over. Simo Miskovic hardly said anything. Arsic, Zeljaja, and some of the security officers were the ones who talked, as did Kuruzovic. They talked about war. They said we didn't know what war was. They recommended that we all got in a vehicle and they could drive us to the front so we could finally see what war meant. Zeljaja then took over. And he gave an ultimatum, saying that the weapons needed to be surrendered. It was an impossible ultimatum. Beco said that we weren't armed in a way that they thought we were armed. They said they knew exactly how many weapons we had. And they mentioned certain numbers. Arsic or Zeljaja gave us one number, then somebody from the security gave another figure. Somebody said there were 10- to 11.000 barrels in Prijedor, 5- to 7.000 in Kozarac, and either way, they wanted these thousands of weapons to be surrendered. They said that conversation could continue only after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: How many weapons did the non-Serb population have at that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very, very few. In a military sense, nothing. As far as infantry weapons are concerned, there might have been a few dozen pieces. But there were quite a few hunting rifles, because during peacetime, a lot of the people were hunters. There were quite a few personal pistol, personal weapons, rifles from the Turkish era and some improvised devices that look like a rifle. However, when you put it all together it wouldn't have been more than a thousand pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you and the other members of the SDA delegation explain this to the members of the Serb delegation at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beco gave this explanation, Bahonjic was also explaining things. However, they interrupted us in our explanations and at one point Zeljaja was very aggressive in saying, We know exactly how many weapons you have. If Kozarac doesn't return - I can't remember whether said 5- or 7.000 pieces - I will flatten Kozarac with the ground. Serbian police must be in Kozarac and the Serbian flag must be in Kozarac. Run your weapons, and when the Serbian police and Serbian flag are in Kozarac, we will sit down and talk. Beco of course said, People is it clear to you that we do not have those weapons? And he said, Well, that's your problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: During this meeting, how did the members of the Serb delegation refer to the Kozarac TO and the Kozarac police? Did they use any particular names to refer to them?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zeljaja, the man I talked about, and Arsic, they talked about the Green Berets. They said, We know how Green Berets there, how many weapons there are, and so on. He was using only that term, Green Berets, or the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were there any Green Berets in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there weren't. There weren't any Green Berets. There wasn't any army. It was the -- an attempt to create the Territorial Defence, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how did the meeting end that day?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It ended with this ultimatum, the threat; namely that we had to return these thousands of pieces of weapons than the Serbian army or the Serbian police had to take over Kozarac and the Serbian flag had to fly over Kozarac. A key problem was that at the very same moment we knew that there was no theoretical chance for us to meet this ultimatum because we didn't have that number of weapons, and if we returned fewer weapons than in the ultimatum, that would have meant that we failed to meet the conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: After this meeting, did you and the other SDA leaders convey what happened in this meeting to the community leaders in the Kozarac and the surrounding non-Serb areas?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We informed them. People were given the information in the atmosphere that I already described. There was no way out, and we were given an impossible ultimatum. We told this to the people. We discussed it. And the people saw only one single problem with this, which was how to protect the lives of the people. There wasn't anything positive that we could say about the conduct of the Serbs. There were these types of ultimatums. However, we knew that there were not even minimal guarantees provided by those who had issued the ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see it's almost time for a break. Perhaps it's a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we would resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Prior to the break, we were talking about a meeting that you attended with the community leaders in Kozarac following this meeting you had with the SDS leadership and members of the military and police in Prijedor. Can you tell us what actions the leadership in Kozarac decided to take at this point in time, having learned what went down at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The leadership continued to try to keep in touch and to try and talk to the SDS leadership and the valid municipal structures again. There were attempts to contact them in Banja Luka and from what was done in the field, it was clear that the threats were serious, so attempts were made to increase the security of the population. There were attempts to organise the Territorial Defence in a way that would reduce tensions and reduce fear among the population. However, there were attempts during the entire time not to cause any provocations, not to provoke the SDS structures and the powers that it had.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] It was on. I don't know why it didn't work that time. You mentioned that there were attempts to organise the TO in the Kozarac area. Can you tell us what attempts were made? What was the first thing that the people of Kozarac tried to do?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people from Kozarac, at the time that it became clear that it was impossible to answer an ultimatum of that type, the only thing that remained was to take all measures in order to protect the lives of the civilians and of the population. The only structure that existed and for which there were orders on the republican level, were the remains of the TO located in the Kozarac area and in a small area outside of Prijedor in the area of Hambarine, Rizvanovici and Ljubija. These were the only territories where some indirect structures of Bosnia-Herzegovina existed at the time. The conclusion was that the TO had to expand and be organised in a way to protect the population from being massacred, should that ever happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you've said that the decision was made to try to expand the TO. What was the first step in that process?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In an establishment sense, in peacetime conditions, the TO had a minimal number of men. It was necessary to expand this, in order to be able to achieve at least minimal protection and to organise the people who were able to obtain any sort of weapons, in order to protect the population. The only legal way was to expand the TO in an establishment sense, and this was done during those days; however, not through mobilisation but through volunteering. People weren't ordered to join. People reported on their own, or they asked to join the Territorial Defence because they were not able to sit at home afraid and in the uncertainty without any organisation that that would serve to protect their homes. Based on the records that we had, lists were very soon put together, and since we didn't know what number of people we had, and we had no vital information in relation to the defence, people were told to put themselves on the list, as well as the weapons that they had, if they had any, and then various formations were put together from this pool of people, based on the structure of the TO, with the Main Staff in Kozarac and with regional staffs in the various local communities, or at -- or at even lower levels if the local communities were large. And let me just say this: This was only an attempt because we didn't manage to put together a list of all those people who volunteered to join the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, if I might interrupt briefly. You're probably aware of this, as is the Chamber, but the -- when we take the usual break at 12.05, would you have left only seven minutes of your total allotted time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just to clarify, you mentioned these lists of volunteers were created. Did you sign the list?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did sign the list and everybody from my village signed, or at least the majority did. And I must say that people of other ethnicities also signed this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you own a weapon at that time?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that this was merely an attempt to expand the TO. Were the non-Serbs in Kozarac area, in the end, able to really organise a defence before the Serbs attacked that area?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not. The time was very short, and we failed to complete the organisation which could have been effective. It was broken up practically within a few hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you explain why you weren't able to mobilise in that time-period. Obviously it a limited time-period of a week or two. But what other barriers were there with regard to mobilising the TO.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were completely isolated. Communication was very poor or impossible. There were no communications devices. There were no weapons. You would be able to defend half of a village and then there would be an open area of several kilometres completely unprotected and then again a few rifles in a part of a village. There weren't enough weapons, there weren't enough professionals who would be able to do this. There were only two or three officers for the 20.000 or so people. There wasn't enough time. There wasn't any fuel. We simply didn't have the available resources to do this, not even in a longer period of time, let alone such a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: By the time of the Serb attack on Kozarac, at maximum, how many men had been mobilised into the Kozarac TO?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number of people. There might have been 2- or 3.000. But the vast majority of them were unarmed, including people who had very old style pistols and personal weapons, the maximum number of people who were armed in the TO would have been about a thousand for the entire area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And that is for the entire Kozarac area, including Trnopolje? Or which areas are you covering with that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the entire area of Kozarac, all the local communities, this entire non-Serb area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were any plans made to attack Prijedor town or any of the Serb areas in the municipality during this period of mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were any plans made to attack any Serb military, VRS, or TO units in the Prijedor area during this period?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we look at P653.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What you have before you is a dispatch from SJB Prijedor to CSB Banja Luka dated 18 May 1992. We see that listed in this -- and we need to zoom out a little bit. Listed in this dispatch are a number of local communes. Can you tell us what are the ethnicities or the ethnic majorities of these communities listed here, just generally?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the non-Serb ethnicity who are in a majority, so in Rizvanovici, Hambarine, and Biscani, mostly there were Bosniaks. In Carakovo as -- too. Now the areas of Kozarac and Kozarusa was inhabited mostly by the Bosniak population, though some local communes had mixed population, but all in all this was non-Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now we see in the first paragraph it is written that -- or refers to paramilitary units present in these local communes. Can you tell us other than the -- first of all, were there any non-Serb paramilitary units in the Kozarac area?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. There was only the Territorial Defence and nothing else. And there was the police, with its reserve force. That was it. However, the Serb authorities referred to all of them as paramilitaries in relation to their own structure, the para state structure that they set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, for Kozarac and Kozarusa, the report states that there this is a unit the size of a company with rifles and mortars. Can you tell us how big is a company?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't in the infantry, but a company can number several hundred men, at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And was this an accurate estimation of the size of the TO units in the Kozarac area before the attack on Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now your previous answer --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Let me just add that, so far as the weapons are concerned, this isn't accurate. If hunting rifles and such-like are meant under weapons, then it's true. As far as I know, there were no mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now in your prior answer you mentioned -- that prior to the attack on Kozarac, you mentioned the number of 2.000 -- I think you mentioned about 1.000 persons. A company is less than a thousand persons. Can you explain the discrepancy? What were you referring to when you said that a thousand people were in the TO?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were quite a few people without weapons. There were very many of those who had pistols. A significant number of people had old-fashioned pistols or makeshift contraptions. So if we added all of these together, pistols, and old-fashioned pistol, whatever could be used for combat, and if we add all the people together, and some of them were unusable in war, then we could have a thousand people. But as for the proper infantry weapons, there were a few of those. But if I can make an observation. This document, dated the 14th of May, does not tally in any of its elements with what they were telling us at the meeting where we were issued with an ultimatum. From what I can see, there is an official document. The people who were members of this structure are asked that we should give back 5- to 7.000 rifles. Evidently, they knew what the situation was like when it came to the number of weapons, but they deliberately placed before us impossible requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I want to make sure we understand you properly on this issue. If I understand you correctly, in the Kozarac area, there may have been somewhere around a thousand weapons. However, for the Kozarac TO itself, there was only units about the size of a company which is, I think you said, several hundred people at most that had been mobilised by the time of the attack?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence was attempted to be put together based on the list of volunteers who signed their names on that list. There was no time to take it a step further from that list. What we knew, based on these lists, was that when we factored in all these makeshift contraption old-fashioned pistols, M48 rifles, automatic or semi-automatic rifles, when we put all these together we couldn't have more than a thousand men. As for the conventional formation of a unit with automatic weapons I don't think we had more than a -- several hundred of those. However, in the documents you have before the Tribunal, you can easily find out what the numbers were.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at 1D312.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is an intelligence report dated 3 June 1992. In the first part, it lists members of a -- four squads that purportedly made up the Trnopolje platoon of the Patriotic League. Was the Patriotic League in the Trnopolje-Kozarac area at this time, prior to the attack on Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Some of the people mentioned in these lists were members of the Territorial Defence. Some of them were; others were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Are there any minors or elderly listed here?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, Suad Sivac was a minor and he is listed as having an automatic rifle, and I know for a fact that he did not have a weapon because he is my friend's brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It mentions in this report a Kozarac Crisis Staff. Was a Crisis Staff ever established in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. Some referred to the TO Staff as the Crisis Staff. It was a term that was widely used to refer to all these structures in that period of time. But in proper legal terms, a Crisis Staff was never set up, one that would have a stamp, powers, and order issuing authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: During the three-week -- well, first of all, I think you have already mentioned that after the takeover the meeting was --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, one other thing I would like to observe. There are people listed here as having weapons who did not have them at all. Huso Trnjanin, the friend of mine and a neighbour, didn't have any weapons. And he was about to come of age. And he is listed here as having had an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I think you mentioned this, but after the takeover, who controlled the media in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, even before the takeover, it was the SDS that controlled the media. The main television outlets were held by the SDS months before the takeover. As for the local media, after the takeover, they were taken by the SDS and were under their exclusive control. All the non-Serb employees were prohibited from working at "Kozarski Vjesnik" and other such media.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In the three-week period between the takeover the Prijedor and the attack on Kozarac, how were members of the SDA and HDZ leadership portrayed through the media in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the takeover, they started referring to us as extremists. They referred to the Territorial Defence as the Patriotic League at first, and later as the Ustasha forces, as the Muslim Mujahedin forces, as the Muslim army, regardless of the fact that there were people of other ethnicities in them as well. At the point when they took over the power by force, they referred to us as the Ustasha, as the Ustasha Mujahedin forces. They referred to the politicians as the fundamentalists, the extremists, et cetera. These were all manner of derogatory terms from the vocabulary of the propaganda that had been employed previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Prior to the attack on Kozarac, were there any serious acts of violence against the non-Serb population in this area?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. There were speculations or accusations from the Serbian authorities that somebody had killed a Serb policeman in an area of Prijedor. It was alleged that this individual fled to the area inhabited by the Bosniaks. However, details were never shed light on by the police. Still the allegations remained that it was the Muslims who had done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I think you misunderstood my question. Prior to the attack on Kozarac, was there any incidents of violence against the non-Serb population? Were there any shelling incidents or such before the attack on Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, on what date was Kozarac attacked?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kozarac was attacked, I believe, on the 24th of May. I think it was the 24th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In the days prior to the attack on Kozarac, were there any ultimatums issued to the people of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several ultimatums of sorts. After the meeting I attended, I know that another team went to Prijedor to negotiate the modalities of surrender. They went there twice. Shortly before the attack when they went there, they never returned. We learnt at later date that they had been liquidated. After this, there were no more contacts, and a day or two later, an attack followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This delegation that went to Prijedor to negotiate, who was a member of that delegation?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The delegation was led by the chief of police in Kozarac, that's to say of the regular police. His name was Osman. We referred to him as Osmo. I don't remember his surname. We all knew him as Osmo. He was the Kozarac police commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And at this -- this delegation, at this point what were they prepared to do? What were they prepared to offer the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last time they went, they did so in order to discuss the modalities of the arms surrender. They wanted the police to come visit and see for themselves what the quantities of weapons involved were. That was the basic reason why they went to Prijedor. The previous discussions in Banja Luka and discussions with the SDS failed, and this was the only thing that was left to be done. The last-ditch chance to prevent an attack. But they did not succeed. They simply never returned from this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So, at that stage, the Kozarac TO was prepared to surrender any weapons they had. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The last-but-one time when Osman and the Bahonjic led this delegation, I don't know what the substance of their discussions back there was but when they returned they told us that we simply will to meet their demands. They gave their proposal that they should come and visit these areas and see for themselves. They had hoped that the proposal would be accepted. We don't know what they discussed subsequently. We only know that they were liquidated.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, at what time on May 24th did the attack on Kozarac begin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, I would like to clarify something. At 39, line -- no at 40; 40, line 2, the witness seemed to have said when I read the record that the delegation, "They simply never returned from this meeting." And that's in clear contradiction with what he says a few lines after that. Could you please clarify whether the witness meant -- really meant this?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, you've mentioned that a delegation went to Prijedor to negotiate the arms surrender and that they were liquidated. You also mentioned that a delegation returned to Kozarac and told you that -- that the Serbs refused to discuss it and that they -- they demanded that their demands be met. Can you kindly explain that contradiction for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I first wanted to describe for you the time-line and then the two delegations. Both delegations, on both occasions, were led by the police chief Osmo. When Osmo went with Bahonjic and some others to Prijedor for the first time, they had their meeting, they had their discussion and then returned. They had consultations locally, and then a day or two later they went there again to negotiate the modalities of surrender, and it was after that second visit that they never returned. But it's always the time group of people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you say after the second meeting they never returned. Mr. Olmsted said something about liquidation, were they -- was that what was happening -- happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were not sure that they had been liquidated. We didn't have any information. We presumed that they were detained or put in prison. They did not return to Kozarac and we didn't have any contact with them. It was only later on that we found out that they had been liquidated. The remains of some of them have not been uncovered to this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, at what time on the 24th of May did the attack on Kozarac begin?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 24th of May, the attack began at around noon. At 11.00, I think, I set out for Kozarac. There was short lull in the shelling, which resumed after noon and it was an all-out shelling from all directions. At that point, I was about to enter Kozarac. I was there for about a half an hour and went back to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If I understand your last answer, did the shelling begin before 11.00 a.m.? Because you said there was a lull in the shelling. Can you explain that a little further.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shelling started at about 11.00 in the morning. We could hear shells landing on Kozarac. Then there was a pause of perhaps half an hour or an hour, I can't be sure, which was followed by fierce unrelenting shelling from all directions on Kozarac and the villages beyond Kozarac. The area across from the road, across from Kozarac, was not shelled. I was, by that time, very close to the area that was hit by shells. I was there for half an hour and then went back to Trnopolje because I could not reach the TO staff in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Before the shelling begin, did the Serb authorities in Prijedor or the military issue -- or, first of all, did they allow the non-Serb women, children and elderly to leave Kozarac before the shelling began?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. As the first shells impacted, there were victims in the yards and on the roads. Later on, people started fleeing, and as they did so, many perished under artillery fire. Actually, there was chaos, people fleeing in all sorts of directions and crossing their paths, one another's path, and the shelling of Kozarac lasted for two days and two nights, with some short interruptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did the non-Serb population, either the Kozarac TO or the population in general, offer any resistance to the shelling? Did they fire shells back or do anything?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None. They didn't have anything to resist with. They didn't have infantry weapons, let alone artillery. Not even trenches had been dug to protect people from artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And where did you go after the shelling ended? You said the shelling lasted for two days and two nights. Where did you go after the shelling ended?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the shelling ended, the population started fleeing from Trnopolje because the infantry troops were on their way from Prijedor to Trnopolje and killing people on their way. The population was fleeing in the direction of Kozarac. I followed them. On the second night I was in the village of Suhi Brod, on the Trnopolje-Kozarac road, quite close to the vantage point from which I was able to observe shelling two days earlier. In the evening hours of that second day, the mass torching of non-Serb areas began from the direction of Prijedor. In a very short span of time, along the length of several kilometres, several villages and hamlets were set on fire. Houses in the village of Mujkanovici, Kozarusa, and the suburbs of Kozarac were on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who way torching these villages, these non-Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb infantry advancing from Prijedor. They followed artillery and killed off the elderly who weren't fast and able to flee. They set houses on fire even where inhabits were still in the homes. We had eye-witnesses who fled that area and we know for a fact that the infantry that was advancing killed Asim Melkic, an elderly person who was unable to walk fast. They would first hurl hand-grenades into those houses where they presumed there was still people and then they would hurl special sort of bombs that were able to set houses on fire. So the two villages were on fire in a very brief period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned you saw the infantry there. Did you see any member of the civilian police participating in these operations in these non-Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. In the following days during their operations of ethnic cleansing, there were several formations that were part of these groups, including soldiers in blue, and I mean dark blue uniforms; there were soldiers wearing conventional military uniforms; there were those who -- who had only parts of uniform and the rest were civilian clothes. There was a blue APC which I was able to see from quite close-up. It wasn't in the olive-drab colour. It was purple-blue in colour and I could see soldiers wearing different insignia. I don't know which units they belonged to establishment-wise. I can only tell you the sort of uniform I saw them wearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: How many of these operations following the shelling of the Kozarac area did you personally witness? You were around the Kozarac area during this time-period. Which ones did you actually see for yourself?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I was at a boundary where three villages coming together, I was able to saw [as interpreted] from quite close-up the ethnic cleansing as it was taking place and I was able to observe it on three occasions. Naturally, I was hidden. I was hidden in a way that I could possibly be. The scenario was more or less identical. They would encircle the area from three sides, from an intersection from meadows and then fire would be opened from all directions, all at once. People would start fleeing. They would kill individuals, one or two individuals per village or hamlet normally. Then they would then advance whilst shooting. They would gather the population normally next to one of the larger houses. Next, they would take the men to the vehicles that were already standing ready on the road.
