In the situations where they didn't have vehicles, they would escort them either toward Kozarac or toward Trnopolje on foot. In all these three instances, things happened the same way. There would always be a couple of dead bodies left behind. During the night, one or two houses would be set on fire, and then the remaining women and children frightful -- frightful, had to pack their belongings and leave the area in droves.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you name the three villages that you personally witnessed these operations being conducted?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sivci, Gornji Sivci, Mujkanovici, and Dergici [phoen] and part of Suvi Brod or Ornici, and another hamlet I can't remember right now, Muranovici, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you mentioned that after they encircled these villages and opened fired on them, they were rounding up the men. Were the non-Serb villagers in these locations offering any kind of resistance to their arrest or to these attacks?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. No one anywhere in the area where I was. Because in the days before, after the ultimatum, people gathered the arms that they had and they turned them over at the municipality building in Trnopolje where the Serb police and the army had already entered. I know one of our neighbours was collecting the weapons, Redzo together with a man from Sivci village whose name I don't know. And already on the second day after the shelling of Kozarac, the weapons had been turned over. These were purely columns of refugees. There was no resistance but still the cleansing continued. Villages were emptied and people ran away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, just one minute, please. Mr. Witness, you said you were observing things from a place where you were hiding. Did you see all this happening in this -- in these different hamlets from the same hiding place? Were able to see all that from one hiding place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was moving around within an area, within a diameter of, say, 300 metres. Within those 300 metres, there was the boundary between three villages. There was an old barn some 10 metres from the road from --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... so I had not-- had time to -- farther away. The second time I tried to run. Soldiers on APCs had already come and I managed to run just a bit further away into the berry bushes next to the road, and I watched through the berries people being led, captured. And the third time I watched from the house of Dzemal Sivac. As this operation of theirs had begun, I had not time to run away. I lay on the roof of the house and watched. I saw the Mujkanovici village being surrounded and when they took away 17 men, first these men were gathered outside one of the houses and then they were led along the roads that I was watching. They all passed by that house and I even heard what the soldiers were ordering them to do. They ordered them to sing some songs. They beat some of the men. But all of them with their arms raised were taken away in the direction of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned soldiers. Did the police also -- the civilian police also participate in these arrests of these non-Serb men in these villages?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In one case that I watched all of them were wearing regular army uniforms. In another case, it was a mixed group, a few police uniforms and about ten soldiers. So ten soldiers and perhaps only two police uniforms. There were also two or three Martic's policemen from the Serbian Krajina in Croatia. The rest were wearing regular army uniforms. And the third incident I mentioned, apart from the uniforms I already described, there were two men who were wearing only parts of military uniform. One was wearing jeans, if I remember well, with an army shirt. And the other one was wearing trainers, not army boots. And I was so close that I could even hear them talking to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned that during the operations non-Serb homes were torched, set on fire. Were any Serb homes destroyed during these operations?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, by no means. Not a single one. Those Serb houses which were inside non-Serb territory had been given instructions to mark their houses in white paint with a large letter S, and that was a sign to the soldiers who were involved in this operation that I described to pass that house by, to leave it alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And during these operations, what happened to non-Serb movable property, their possessions that they had in their houses?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the expulsion of women and children and the last stragglers, the next day began the looting. In fact, at first, I thought those were robberies, but two days into it, I realised it was systematic. Teams arrived carrying out only one type of property, such as a team taking away household appliances. Then another team would arrive taking different sorts of items, televisions, VCRs, technical equipment. Then other teams came, taking away woodwork, chandeliers, whatever was of good quality. But they all stored it in one and the same place. And then trucks would arrive and take it in the direction of Kozarac. So this plundering was selective. And only when that was finished, individual looters would come and take what remained in the houses, or they would come with carts and take it all away.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What happened to your own home in Trnopolje during this period?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My house was not torched. It was rifled and plundered, yes. It was ransacked, but it was not torched. In the very centre of Trnopolje, the army did not torch or plunder houses. In the very centre, within a diameter of about 500 metres houses were left intact, but the population was expelled, and very soon afterwards, some Serbs took over these houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us, you said you personally observed three of these probations but you were in the community for quite some time. How long did these cleansing operations last?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And by the end of these operations, how many non-Serbs remained in the Kozarac area?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no one remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at 65 ter 476. This is tab 2. And if we can turn to page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see this is a dispatch from SJB Prijedor to CSB Banja Luka dated 5 July 1992. If you look first at item number 2 it states that: "According to the disarmament plan, the search was supposed to start on 22 May 1992?" Were you aware that two days before the attack on Kozarac the Bosnian Serb police had intended to enter Kozarac and search for weapons?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't know that. I saw that for the first time when this paper was shown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we look at item number 3, it provides as a reason for the start of the war in Kozarac, as it says: "... was the blockade of the Prijedor-Banja Luka main road as well as the attack on the military column during negotiations on the unconditional returns of weapons belonging to paramilitary formations." You already mentioned there was a couple last-ditch efforts to -- by a non-Serb delegation to surrender the TO weapons. At the same time did the Kozarac TO mount an attack on the VRS column along this Prijedor-Banja Luka road?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, to be quite honest, I don't believe it. I don't know believe it for two reasons. Sometime before this, the Serb army put up a tank at the entrance to Kozarac. No one even tried to come near those soldiers in the tank crew, let alone hurt them. I heard that there were some forces from Jakupovici but they were coming in shooting and the orders were not to shoot except in self-defence. I don't think anyone opened fire at the Serbs without being fired at first. And another thing, that road had been blocked for a long time before by the Serb army and when these combat operations of theirs started people probably had to defend themselves. What exactly happened there, I don't know. I wasn't there. But we had at that point no more co-ordination for me to be able to find out the details. I only heard on the Serb radio that the army had been attacked in Jakupovici and that because of that, the army was taking action.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This item further states that the fighting started with an artillery attack and then members of the army and police embarked on mopping up the terrain. Are these the cleansing operations that you described for us a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And then it states that in the course of these operations, citizens collected weapons themselves and handed them over to the army and police. I think you mentioned that you witnesses this in at least one village. So the non-Serb population was co-operating with the army and the police during these operations?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was not one village. That happened in Hadzici in Sivci in Kenjari village, in Trnopolje. That was the pattern in a large number of villages. I was present during one such collection of weapons in Sivci village.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now item number 7 lists the number of weapons collected and seized as of the date of this July dispatch. And I have added them up myself, and I arrived at a total of about one thousand weapons seized not only in Kozarac but Hambarine and other non-Serb areas in Prijedor. So that is, would you agree, consistent with your estimate that there was less than a thousand weapons or around a thousand weapons at most in the Kozarac area in the possession of the non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That is consistent with my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did anyone from the Prijedor SJB confirm to you that they knew that the citizens of Kozarac did not have many weapons?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The inspector in Omarska confirmed it by the name of Dragan Radakovic. He is the one who interrogated me in Omarska camp. In fact, that is the first thing he said when I came in to be questioned. He said verbatim, listen, Sejmenovic, we're not interested in weapons, we know you didn't have weapons. There was a very small amount, negligible. We're interested in Sarajevo. We're interested in SDA policy, the government, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: On what basis, Mr. Olmsted?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, we just went through a number of the items and this witness could confirm certain information and clarify and contradict other information in it. Therefore, I think since he has been able to speak about it - there is probably no objection on authenticity grounds - we move to admitted it at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do not mean to object immediately to the admission of this document, but it is precisely as you said. We have the evidence of this witness, second-hand hearsay in some cases. At the time when this document was drafted, he was in hiding. He had nothing to do with the writing of the document. He doesn't know to whom it was sent, nor had he seen it before proofing. We have thus his evidence on one of the facts mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01717, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I now want to show you a video that you had an opportunity to review during proofing. It's 65 ter 3598. And it's an ABC "Nightline" programme. And if we can go to 5 minutes and 40 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: "Dave Marish: ... we visited the ethnically cleansed Kozarac in northern Bosnia last week. We were closely supervised by the local Serb militia, restricted to just a few blocks of the town" --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Pause right here, about 5 minutes and 53 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: First of all, do you recognise this village that is depicted in this footage?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one house that you see just as you come into Kozarac from the road to Banja Luka. It's at the first intersection.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall, is this a non-Serb house or a Serb house?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no Serb houses there. Only Bosniaks live there. I think it's either in this house or the -- the house next to this one that the Lovic family lived. In any case, in this case there was no Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can we continue with the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: "Dave Marish: ... home to about 15.000 Muslim men, women and children. Today there are no Muslims there, none, and none of their X-marked homes is intact. Other homes in Kozarac" --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Pause at 6 minutes and 8 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: First of all, the houses that we looked at before, the ones that appear to be damaged, were those non-Serb houses as well?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not. Some houses that were torched later were either Serb houses or houses that the soldiers appropriated. With Serb houses, the rule was that they would mark them. This Mirko Djurdjevic may be the name of the soldier who took over the house, or it was originally owned by a Serb, Mirko Djurdjevic. It's one of the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to clarify your last answer. It says here in the transcript that Serb houses were torched. Were any Serb houses torched in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. There were a few non-Serb houses but were not torched.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Again, the record says: "There were a few non-Serb houses but they were not torched." Do you mean there are were a few Serb houses that were not torched? Because your answer is confusing based on what you said earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This is exactly what the witness said. It was properly interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Then I just need the witness to explain that a little bit better.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your answer was that: "There were a few non-Serb houses," so Bosniak or Croat houses, "that were not torched." I see, I misread your answer. So you're saying there were a few non-Serb houses that were preserved, that they weren't actually destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe there is a confusion in interpretation. When the infantry came into Kozarac, they torched almost all the houses. When they came to a house that they knew was owned by a Serb, they spared it. They didn't set it on fire. So Serb houses were not set on fire. Some of the army troops that came into Kozarac included residents of Kozarac, Serbs, so they preserved some houses in the centre, mainly Serb houses. Or, they appropriated them. And they also did not allow some non-Serb houses to be torched because they wanted to take these houses for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. I think it was my confusion. If we can continue a little bit further.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: "Dave Marish: ... have been marked to survive. This one with the colours of the Serbian flag. This --"

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We just paused at 6 minutes and 14 seconds, but just a moment before we saw a house with the Serbian flag painted on it. And here we are, we have it in front of us at 6 minutes, 11 seconds. Why would someone paint a Serbian flag on a house?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a house where a Serbian family lives, or a Serb, at this moment in any case, and then that Serb would either put up a Serbian flag or write on the house, This is Serbian, because, at the time, non-Serb houses were being torched and looted to protect himself from the torching and looting, this owner wrote on the house that it was Serbian or put up the flag and/or would also put a board with his Serbian name on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can we continue with the footage then.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: "David Marish: ... with the colours of the Serbian flag. This one says: 'This is Serbian!' They stand undamaged like the remaining Serb" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "David Marish: -- residents of Kozarac surrounded in silence, deadly silence."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. Can we stop it there. Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, can we have the indication of the date when this was filmed, if it's known?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. It was filmed late in 1992, was when it was filmed. I think in the transcript there's reference that this footage was a few months after -- after the attack on Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if it's late in 1992 how would the answer -- how would the -- this witness be able to comment on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, he just commented on it. He was describing the destruction in Kozarac. We saw some of the destruction in this video. We saw the painting of a flag on a Serb -- a house that was occupied by a Serb so it would not be destroyed, and, in fact, was not destroyed. So it corroborates his evidence as to what was happening in Kozarac during the attack, after the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you're -- Mr. Olmsted, with all due respect, if you are trying to -- to rephrase the -- what the -- what the newspaper person or the journalist was saying, we heard that. Now, the -- the witness cannot only confirm what we saw here. He wasn't there. He doesn't know -- he knows one -- I believe one house he only recognised it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I thought I heard the journalist saying at the very beginning of the footage that we saw that he and his team visited Kozarac a few days after the attack. But maybe you could hear it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is precisely why I asked when this was filmed. Because it -- it might be significant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, we can go back -- why don't we go back to the beginning. It's at 5 minutes and 40 seconds and play it from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: "Dave Marish: ... area dominated by two cities, Prijedor and Banja Luka and a once thriving Muslim town called Kozarac. We visited the ethnically cleansed Kozarac in northern Bosnia last week. We were closely supervised by the local Serb militia, restricted to just a few blocks of the town, once home to about 15.000 Muslim men, woman and children. Today there are no Muslim there, none, and none of their X-marked homes is in tact. Other homes in Kozarac have been marked to survive. This one with the colours of the Serbian flag. This one says 'This is Serbia!' They stand undamaged like the remaining Serb residents of Kozarac surrounded in silence, deadly silence. "Where are all the ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe in the transcript which covers the entire ABC "Nightline" programme, Ted Koppel states at the beginning that the footage was -- I believe I will have to look for the reference, it was a few months after the attack actually occurred. But I can simply clarify this matter with this witness as to whether he saw this kind of damage in Kozarac itself and whether it was during that time-period that this damage occurred, if that's the objection by the Defence as to what -- what this witness particularly knew had happened in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, in your list of documents, the video is dated November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And that would be consistent with what I was assuming. I have to -- I would have to read through the entire transcript to confirm that, but I think that is my recollection as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But let me ask you, sir, before we break: You were in -- in the area of Kozarac. You saw this footage. Was this level of damage to the non-Serb property what you witnessed yourself in Kozarac and the surrounding areas, after the -- after the shelling that took place at the end of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, I think this is leading. We would need an open question for this witness, if we are to satisfy the requirement properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'll rephrase, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: How did what you saw on this video compare to the damage that you saw in Kozarac and the surrounding areas during and after the shelling in May and June 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I really want to be of assistance. Houses were marked like this and we saw it practically the day after the ethnic cleansing. The army walked through and some -- it would leave marks behind. The Serbs would receive information that they needed to mark their houses, and they did so. Another important fact, in order to understand this issue, the woman who helped me hide in Gornji Sivac [phoen] told me something that a mobilised soldier, a Ukrainian, had told her; namely, that she need to put the letter S on her house, as well as the soldier across the road, so that when the army passed through they would leave her house alone. And this was really what happened. There was a large letter S on the house across the road. The wife of Dzemal Sivac also put a large S on her house, and the houses around were torched or fire was opened on them. However, the soldiers left her house alone. The same markings happened in other villages, in Trnopolje where I lived, in Trnjani. Similar markings were made by the Serbs who moved into those homes in the recent days. And what I remember is similar to what's on the footage. And what was done here is similar to what was done in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry -- I'm terribly sorry, I just ... have an intervention, 58, line 8. I believe I heard the witness saying, "The mobilised soldier who was Ukrainian." Can you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The place where I was hiding is on the boundary of three villages, and in one of those villages there are some non-Serbian families where Ukrainians lived. Since Trnopolje was very mixed ethnically. And these Ukrainians had received very serious threats that they were either to be mobilised into the Serbian army or they would encounter the same problems as others. And the neighbour of the woman who helped me hide accepted to be mobilised. He took a rifle, he put on the uniform, but he asked not to be included in operations and instead to be allowed to be on duty service around houses, and he did that for a few days until he was told the following, verbatim: You are not loyal. When you kill a few Muslims we will know that you are loyal to us. He was very frightened by this. There was a family in the area that was Bosniak. And I remember that a few times he went out and opened fire on -- in the corn field when he heard a noise, hoping that he would hit somebody who was hiding there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think the main point with regard to this video is this witness was able to identify that this is Kozarac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted. My initial hesitation was that I was trying to remind myself as to how we would have dealt with these news -- bits of news footage previously, but clearly the purpose of tendering it is that it is illustrative of the witness's testimony. And the witness's explanation at 58, line 16 through 18, what I remember is similar to what is on footage and what was done there clarifies everything. So the matter -- the footage may be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01718, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I see it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. And you will wind up when we return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We have a brief oral ruling which we would deliver while the witness is on his way in. In its oral ruling of the 12th of November, 2010, the Trial Chamber, inter alia, denied the Prosecution's motion to admit the evidence of ST-223, pursuant to Rule 92 bis. The Trial Chamber ordered ST-223 to be called viva voce and granted the Prosecution 45 minutes to conduct its examination-in-chief. On the same day, the Prosecution orally requested the Trial Chamber to reconsider its decision as to time and to allow the Prosecution to examine the witness for the full four hours, as requested, arguing that the witness is called to cover a huge all encompassing fact and that he comes at it from a different angle than ST-224 who will cover the same denied adjudicated fact. The Trial Chamber is still not persuaded that the Prosecution needs four hours to address the contents of Fact 193, considering that similar evidence has been already elicited from other witnesses. Nevertheless, in the interests of justice, the Trial Chamber has reconsidered its decision in light of the Prosecution's new submission on the unique vantage point of ST-223. The Trial Chamber will therefore accept the evidence of ST-223 pursuant to Rule 92 ter and admit those portions of ST-223's prior testimony that it considers relevant and unique to the contents of Fact 193, found on the following pages of the transcript tendered: 4398, to 4400, 4402 to 4407, 4409 to 4421, 4427, 4433, and 4436 to 4439. The Trial Chamber finds that the pseudonym sheet of the witness is inseparable and indispensable for his testimony and will therefore also be admitted. The remainder of the proposed associated documents are not admitted. Pursuant to the guide-lines issued in October of 2009, the Trial Chamber grants the Prosecution an additional 25 minutes to examine ST-223, for a total of 45 minutes, to be absorbed within the total time allotted for hearing that denied adjudicated fact witnesses. Pursuant to Rule 92 ter, Witness 223 shall be available for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May we have P1357 on the screen. This is a video. This is ITN footage from August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, please keep your answers short. I only have about eight minute with you left. We are at 1 minute and 34 seconds, and we see -- if we can just play a few seconds of this footage without the sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: There's a man and a woman. Do you recognise the man?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You can pause it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw that man on a few occasions. I believe he was present at the one of the meetings in Prijedor, but I didn't know him personally. Very unique voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was he at the meeting in mid-May 1992 with Simo Miskovic and the other SDS leadership members that you attended?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he was. But he was introduced as one of the security officers. There was one from military security and one from public security. I believe this man was in public security.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could move to 18 minutes and 12 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We're seeing some destroyed houses along the road here. Can you tell us where this footage --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Maybe go back to 18 minutes and 8 seconds, just a little bit further.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the Prijedor-Banja Luka road. I believe it's the area from Kozarac towards Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can just play through the video portion now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us do you know whether these houses that have been destroyed were non-Serb or Serb?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were the property of non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And do you recall when they were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were hit by artillery, then they were torched, and then they were brought down by tanks. And this went on for a few days. All this took place after the attack, seven or ten days after the attack, and the tanks came a little later.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's all I have for this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: After the attack --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, the exhibit number didn't get into the transcript. So if could you -- your tab number or the document number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. It's P1357, tab 17 in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, sir, after the attack in Kozarac, were the non-Serbs required to wear anything to distinguish themselves from the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the attack on Kozarac, I don't know that there were any requests made to the people to wear anything, but I know that there was a request made to groups to hang a white kerchief on a stick and then carry it above their heads. And also they were asked to put a white sheet on their windows if they were at home, as a sign of surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who was issuing this request?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, given our limited time, I want to go right to your time at Omarska. You have already mentioned you were detained there. For how many days were detained at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a few days. Seven to nine days, perhaps. I can't recall exactly. I would need a little time to remember it more clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And that's fine. Approximately when was it this? Can you tell us what part of the month it was?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was around mid-August or the second part of August of 1992, as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who arranged for your release from Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the autonomous region of Krajina, Mr. Vojislav Kupresanin, took me out of Omarska. As far as I could tell, based on his contacts with superiors, he had an order from President Karadzic to find the remaining officials of SDA and take them to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did Kupresanin come to Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: While he was at Omarska camp, and in your presence, did you overhear a telephone conversation he was having with someone?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard some part of what he was saying. First, he talked to me and then a soldier came who told him that the president needed to talk to him on the phone. He answered the phone in the next-door office, and he said that beds and blankets and hygiene things needed to be provided for the camp as soon as possible. And I later realised that he was, in fact, referring to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did you later find out who Mr. Kupresanin was speaking to on the phone?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out when we got to Banja Luka, to his office. He talked to Karadzic on the phone, and he told me that he was talking to Karadzic. He confirmed to Karadzic on the phone that he would provide me with a suit, he would let me rest, he would provide me with food so I could put on some weight, that he would give me money.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did you ever find out why Mr. Kupresanin took you away from Omarska camp? Why were you released?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He asked about other officials as well. He asked me about them, whether they were in Omarska, whether they were alive. He said that we needed to gather them all together and that we should hold round-table meetings to confirm that these weren't just ethnic structures, that we were also to be included so that the population, the non-Serbian population, could be included or could be participate in normal life, and we would have been the representatives of this non-Serbian population. However, most of the leaders were already dead and some had already reached the free territory. We had knowledge of this through the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, in fact, didn't Mr. Kupresanin make you attend a meeting where internationals were present later on in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He took me to a meeting when international mediators arrived to Banja Luka, Lord Carrington and Cyrus Vance. Karadzic also came to Banja Luka together with the entire leadership. Kupresanin took me from Vrbanja to that building in Banja Luka where all these Serbian officials were staying. He told me that I was to meet with President Karadzic but didn't tell me any further details.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did you meet with President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. And he was not happy about. This but, no, the meeting never took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Who wasn't happy about that. Just to clarify?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kupresanin wasn't happy about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you said that Mr. Kupresanin told Mr. Karadzic that you had to put on some weight. Why would he say such a thing? Why -- why did he think you had to weight -- put on weight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because all of us in the camp, especially those who had spent a longer time there, were practically skin and bone, as we say. Everybody was exhausted and very skinny. He said that he needed to put on weight because I couldn't appear at the round-table meetings looking like that for the purpose of these political goals so I needed to recover and look good and then appear in public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Did you lose that much weight in seven or nine days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had lost a lot of weight before, because I lived on my own out in nature, and then I was in the Trnopolje camp and finally in the prison in Omarska, so I lost a lot of weight. Although I -- I am of thin constitution, regardless of my weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Sejmenovic. My name is Aleksandar Aleksic and I am one of the Defence counsel for Mr. Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You testified before this Tribunal in six case, if I have the correct information, in the Tadic, Kovacevic, Sikirica, Stakic, Brdjanin and Krajisnik cases?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In the last case against Mr. Krajisnik, the Defence did not cross-examine you, so only your summary was provided; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I didn't know that -- about that in the Krajisnik case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in late 1990, elections were held in Bosnia for the Republican Assembly, as well as local elections for the Municipal Assemblies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And as you said in this case, you were elected to the Council of Municipalities as a deputy from Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: As for the republican elections, will you agree with me that there were seven electoral unit and that SDS won in Banja Luka and Doboj, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible there must have been some margin but what the margin was, I don't recall. And it didn't have the significance that was ascribed to it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You testified on Friday, I believe, that after the elections local authorities were established in Prijedor. You, as a republican deputy, and you had the right to attend municipal assembly meetings, and you did; however, you did not have the right to vote.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have the right to vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Since we speak the same language, we need to pause for a second before -- between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: If I understood your early evidence and what you said on Friday, you personally, on behalf of your party, the SDA, did not take part in the negotiations about the divisions and the establishment of the government in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not taking part, but I was kept informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Your party was represented in these negotiations by Dr. Mirza Mujadzic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And sometimes the negotiations were led by an authorised delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You know that on behalf of the SDS, the negotiations were led by Mr. Simo Miskovic, President of the Municipal Board?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. When there were talks at the level of the president, then Mujadzic would talk to Miskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: More than once in previous testimony, including Friday in this case, you said these negotiations failed because the SDS would not agree to the appointment of certain SDA candidates to certain positions. They failed because of the intransigent position of the local SDS.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say, Your Honours, it had nothing to do with specific candidates, specific people. It had to do everything with certain departments, certain areas of government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: We will come to that. Last Friday, and in testimony before that, you said that in February -- or, rather, on 17 February 1992, there was an extraordinary session of the Assembly of Prijedor, and on Friday, you mentioned what you said previously in Brdjanin, on page 12307; namely, that the initial demand of the SDS at that assembly session with the assembly be disbanded and that early elections for the municipal assembly be called [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Also in Brdjanin, on 12304, you said you couldn't exactly remember who said what, but you knew that there was a record of that assembly session, and that we could check by looking at that transcript. Therefore, could we see, 65 ter D -- sorry, 2D02-2019. And that is tab 26. I have a hard copy for the witness, because this is a long document, 60 pages in B/C/S. And it might be easier for you to follow on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can have the usher's assistance. It's page 3 in e-court, in B/C/S; and in English, that's page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You see the session was chaired by the president of the municipality, Mr. Cehajic, and that in addition to the assemblymen, 57 of them, there were you, Mr. Mujadzic and Mr. Simo Miskovic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And you can see lower on the same page the agenda, item 1: "Analysis of the implementation of the conclusions of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly session held on 22 January 1992."

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In English, that's the same page. But you should turn to the next page. It says in second paragraph: "The first of the conclusions of that session of the 22nd January 1992 was to charge party presidents and the presidents of Deputies Clubs to divide power within ten days, by the 2nd of February, analyse the previous division and inform the municipal assembly at its next session with the participation of all parliamentary parties. Co-ordination is hereby entrusted to the secretary of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly." You probably know that the secretary was Mr. Dusko Baltic, a lawyer by training.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Now turn to page 43 in B/C/S. In English, it's 28. Mr. Baltic speaks halfway down the page -- sorry, towards the bottom of the page. And he goes on for a while. He says: "I would like briefly to inform the assemblymen on the results of talking held at the meeting of party presidents and the presidents of Deputies Clubs. I am aware that the assemblymen are familiar with the issue and how it ended but I would like to make a formal report about the outcome of that meeting. "Following those conclusions we called a meeting on the 30th of January, and it lasted roughly from 9.00 a.m. to 4.00 p.m. Anticipating certain problems, we decided to record it all on tape, and later we transcribed that tape. I'll just briefly say that after that exhausting meeting no agreement was reached on the division of power, although the representatives of the opposition had tried to help in this discussion, and the outcome of all that was a joint proposal, made at the initiative of all those present, insisting that it be made on behalf of all parties, not just one party, to initiate the motion for dissolving the assembly at this assembly session. So that after debate on the motion, this assembly should adopt a conclusion, in fact a decision, to be submitted to the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina." And then Mr. Cehajic butts in. Because, at this at this point Mr. Popovac, walked out, if you remember. Do you remember that members of the opposition parties, the SDPA, and the liberal party, the former reformists, in other words, were unhappy with the way things were turning out and they walked out of the session?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Popovac, whom you just mentioned was a member of the SDA leadership and he walked out at this moment. Whether he returned later, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: So after that, Mr. Dusko Baltic goes on and says -- next page in English, please: "The proposal was that the assembly, after debating this motion, take a decision to be submitted to the Republic Assembly, which should call early elections. The fourth item" -- This was accepted unanimously, and the meeting ended with applause. Do you remember these words of Mr. Baltic from that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I'm reading the transcript, I -- parts of his speech are coming back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: He was followed by Mr. Suad Kolonic, a deputy from the SDA; right?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: He says: "As far as I know, we, the assemblymen, declared ourselves at the previous session and gave our consent to representatives of Deputies' Clubs, and parties to divide power. We did not, however, authorise them to bid on our behalf on the dissolution of this assembly. In my view, the conclusions that were adopted at their meeting are not binding upon us in any way and finally, Mr. Secretary, who authorised you to send any messages and wires on behalf of all the members of this assembly." Now, on the issue of who was present at that session of the 30th meeting, in fact that meeting, we can refer to the contribution by Mr. Stakic. That's page 49 in B/C/S. In English, it's 32. Sorry, it must be the next page in B/C/S. It's towards the bottom of the page where Mr. Stakic says: "I would just like to enumerate the participants in this agreement, Dr. Mirza Mujadzic, president of the SDA; Professor Husein Crnkic, president of the SDA Deputies Club; Simo Miskovic, president of the SDS; Dragan Savanovic, the president of the SDS Deputies Club. I was there in my own name and on behalf of the assembly, just as the vice-president of the party, then was Aiz, Dragan Svraka, Cedo Vila, Milena Vokic, Nebojsa Bogunovic, Jozo Maricic, Silvije Saric," et cetera. I'll repeat: Cedo Vila, Milena Vokic, Nebojsa Bogunovic, Jozo Maricic and Silvije Saric. So it follows from this that that meeting was attended also by the authorised representatives of the SDA, the president of the municipal board of the party, Mr. Mujadzic and Mr. Crnkic; right?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Now, at the end of that meeting, page 55 in B/C/S and 35 in English, Dr. Mujadzic takes the floor again. It's halfway through this paragraph, he is, in fact, responding to Mr. Miskovic, whom we will read a bit later, and he says: "As for the negotiations that Mr. Miskovic described so exhaustively, the first negotiations that this commission conducted, nobody from this party questions the moral or the professional quality of the negotiations and the team. But, again, neither the commission, nor the party presidents have the authority to say the final word in negotiations. It always goes to the Executive Committee and the Main Board." And he goes on: "In this case, in these papers, the material that we are submitting to you now --" Just one digression. Just before he and Mr. Crnkic spoke and on the 17th of January, he offered the SDA proposal to the SDS as to how to divide power, and he says: "In these papers that we are offering to you now, this material had previously been agreed in the Deputies Club and they are the right papers. They are not in dispute in any way. This is a comprehensive offer. Now if you don't accept this, you can make a counteroffer and then we will try to narrow our differences until we find common ground. I therefore propose that the SDS consider our proposal and their decision, and possibly their counterproposal can then be included as the third item on the next assembly's agenda after the two items that we have proposed which will be analysed by the expert team in co-operation with the executive committee. So the third item could be discussed -- the discussion on the SDA's proposal with a possible SDS counterproposal and the possibility of their further harmonisation." It follows from this, witness, that on that day, the 17th of January, Mr. Mujadzic, from the SDA, or anyone else from the other negotiating teams you mentioned, was not authorised to agree to a specific division of power department by department because it had not been harmonised at the Main Board of the party. Instead, on that day, for the first time, the Municipal Board of the SDA made a formal offer to the SDS on paper, after running this proposal through the Deputies Club, the -- and other authorities of the party. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no I can't agree. You could get that impress though if you are only looking at this. But various offers circulated even before this. This transcript only reflects the moment when the entire political structure of the municipality came to discuss this proposal. This offer that was made to the SDS here had been made before but out of the public eye, outside of the assembly. And this was a moment of confrontation with the public, because the assembly session was broadcast and it was an opportunity for the people to find out what the SDA was offering and what the SDS was refusing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Sir, look at page 27, where Mr. Crnkic takes the floor, the president of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English, that's at page 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Crnkic speaks of the 30 January meeting where he and Mr. Mujadzic agreed that a proposal should be made for early elections and goes on to explain: "After an exhausting debate, we reached an impasse and said, Very well, if there is no other way out, let's have new elections. However, we - I in my capacity as the Deputies Club president, Mirza as the party president, Simo as the SDS president, et cetera - we all have to check our decisions with our boards. It's normal. Whatever we decide must be approved as a proposal by our respective parties, by our respective clubs, by those who brought us here." And then, in the penultimate line, he says: "In this sense, I feel I must intervene here and tell Mr. Svraka what the state of things is; namely, why these conclusions haven't been signed although they have been accepted in principle."

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, based on what Mr. Crnkic, the president of the SDA Deputies Club in the municipal assembly, said, he confirms that Mr. Mujadzic and himself agreed on the meeting on the 30 January as to what the proposal to be placed before the assembly should be but that, however, they had not had the authorisation to sign this before all the relevant party bodies have had a chance to look at it. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before this particular assembly meeting, there were various interpretations circulating of this particular meeting, depending on the party interpreting the meeting. To the best of my knowledge, at this particular meeting where everyone was present, a definitive decision had not been taken. Rather, it was decided that until -- that unless an agreement is reached with the SDS before the next assembly meeting, then it would be up to the assembly to decide the matter. Those were the interpretations, as far as I know. I also know that following this meeting with the opposition, Simo Miskovic no longer wanted to meet with the SDA leadership in an effort to find a solution. On the other hand, the SDA proposal had not yet been made public and this was an opportunity to rectify that. Your Honours, perhaps it would be helpful if, in addition to the quotation you read from what Mr. Crnkic said, to read another sentence of his that followed, so I'm repeating: Crnkic, the head of the Deputies Club is saying, We are in a very chaotic situation and the dissolution of the assembly would only lead to an ever-greater chaos. Why would we want a chaos that is graver than the one we have right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm merely telling you and this is something you will be able to see from Mr. Svraka's address on page 26. Mr. Svraka is a deputy for the liberals which is the former party of reformists of Ante Markovic; right?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was a liberal party and Ante Markovic's reformists were a separate party.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: At any rate, it was not a national party?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But it was in the opposition at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you first what happened and what the time-line of events relating to these conclusions was: "First off, it is true that the conclusion was adopted by all the presidents of parties and presidents of Deputies Clubs after several hours of deliberations. There only remained certain reservations in respect of the matters that were signed. So this is the reason why we should place this matter on today's agenda." Two sentences further down, he goes on to say: "I expect Mr. Mujadzic and Mr. Miljkovic," I think this should read Mr. Miskovic, "to take the floor and tell the people in no uncertain terms if they are ready to agree on matters or not. What they said back at that meeting, they were close to tears. Let me tell you once more that we had reached an agreement at a meeting which took place subsequently, that we would forward these conclusions to the president of the assembly. He summoned us later on to see what the state of affairs was and, at this meeting, we agreed that we would be discussing no other matters but this one. In other words, that the only item on the agenda of the meeting of the assembly on the 17th February would be precisely this matter. A firm promise on this was given by presidents of the parties and presidents of the Deputies Clubs. So what they are doing here today is either a lie or a farce. In my view, it is both. If they do have some sort of trust placed in them by their own respective parties, it is their own matter. However, what we saw happen today and the way this meeting or this session unfolded today, what they should do is leave." It follows from Mr. Svraka's speech that the president of the Municipal Board of the SDA and the president of the Deputies Club agreed at this meeting of the 30th January that the only item on the agenda would be the conclusion around which everyone agreed that early elections were to be called. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, firstly, I'd like you to avoid asking me about the details of the meeting because I did not attend it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Pause there, please. Please turn to page 1 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You misunderstand me. I am talking about the meeting between the opposition and the ruling parties where power-sharing was discussed. I wasn't present at this meeting. I was, however, present at the session of the municipal assembly, the minutes of which we are reading. Thus, who said what at the meeting between presidents of the parties and Deputies Clubs, both the ruling parties and the opposition, I don't know. I only know what the interpretations of the meeting were given by the party presidents at this session. Whether something was agreed, signed, or not signed at the meeting, I cannot tell, because I wasn't there. But I repeat, there were different interpretations of this particular inter-party agreement. There is another matter which is important for the Chamber. Let me explain to you what the proper was: Regardless of the agreement reached by the parties, there was a parliamentary procedure in place. Members of the assembly were not, under the constitution, or any other law, or enactment, duty-bound to adhere to this agreement. They could reach a new conclusion at this assembly meeting, because the conclusions reached at the earlier meeting were pre-dated. As one of the members of the opposition said at this session, Mr. Mujadzic and Mr. Miskovic, sirs, reach an agreement before us here. Or tell us that you cannot reach agreement. According to this deputy's opinion, there was a certain time-limit that was running within which they would have had to reach an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: We will go back to what Mr. Miskovic said later. Mr. Miskovic took the floor immediately before Mr. Mujadzic.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page is that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Give me a moment to find it. It starts at page 51, continues on page 52 through 54. And in English ... pages 33 and 34. At the beginning of his address, and let me make a small digression, it was shortly before he took the floor that Mr. Mujadzic handed him the paper with the proposal of how power should be divided; that's to say, half/half. Mr. Miskovic goes on to say: "I said another thing and it's that some things were done in this way or that way on purpose. I think that Aiz noted it well, and when I react the immediately I was going to propose to the SDA to take all the various departments in order for us to solve the problem and see if this will continue to be the underlying reason or if some other reason will crop up." So what follows from this is that Mr. Miskovic was even prepared to go as far as to offer all of the departments to the SDA, thus handing them over the entire responsibility; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. Mr. Simo Miskovic seized the opportunity to discuss power-sharing in public because there was a radio broadcast being made of this assembly. He was being ironical. He was -- he wanted to make a point of saying that they wanted to go as far as even handing all of the power to the SDA, but what happened, in fact, was that he had been refusing any SDA proposals all along and even the 50-50 percentage division was difficult for him to accept. So he wanted Mr. Mujadzic to speak out and that's why he said what he said here, which did not reflect his own opinion. It was merely a propaganda-driven -- in the direction that was favourable for the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic goes on to say: "If somebody should be laid the blame on, then they should be putting forth some arguments for it. As I see it, all the discussions that have been held here today and that placing the blame on the SDA. I don't know if I'm right, but it has been said that we had not wanted it, that it was obvious who did not want it, that people know who doesn't want it. Now life saving solution has been found proposed by one party. "But let's take things in their proper order. At the beginning of power-sharing, a blockade ensued and therefore we, the SDS, held an ordinary party assembly session electing a new president, and that's to say, myself and my first step was to get in touch with the president of the SDA with a view to removing the cause of the blockade. Talks on that subject were held in the office of the vice-president of the municipal assembly but without the participation the SDA president who had to go away on a trip. However, there was the president of the Deputies Club and the president of the municipal assembly present, and I asked them if they had been given a mandate by their party to negotiate all the various matters and whether the party was going to stand behind our agreement." "There were various discussions on the matter as to whether this was the case or not, and after several hours of discussions the conclusion was that they did not have the mandate. That's number one. These are the facts. "Secondly, when it was established at last that they had not been authorised, we demanded that both parties elect representatives who would be authorised to engage in negotiations who would have the mandate to engage in power-sharing negotiations and thus automatically to lift the blockade of the assembly and who would be the signatories on behalf of their respective parties. That was done. We received a paper stating that among other things, Sefik Krkic would be leading these negotiations on behalf of the SDA, together with the internal revenue service head, Meho and Peso Camil. Right from the start, we defined the criteria based on which we would divide the power. Once the criteria were established, two and a half hours later, without any problems" --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "In an amicable atmosphere, we managed to agree on the 50 -per cent division." He goes on to say: "We agreed that this should -- that a clean copy should be made of it and that on the following day we would complete the second part which would be much easier. "And then it would be forwarded and thus" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, I'm sorry, but is it really necessary to read all this into the transcript? What's the purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do believe it necessary, because it relates to this witness's testimony in this case and in other cases. And it responds to the Prosecution case that the SDS obstructed the process of establishing a government and that it did not take part in the work of the various structures and that all contact had been severed, that they did not take part in government, and that all this happened because of the way the SDS conducted itself; whereas, what I'm just reading out now shows that the story was much different, that the SDA representatives would agree to certain matters but this would later on be reneged because apparently they did not have the adequate authorisation and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But I suppose you will ask -- you will tendered this document. Do you foresee any objections? Because if -- if you tendered it and we -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] ... Your Honour, I have finished with this document. However, in previous cases and on Friday, the witness said that the basic request that the SDS put forth on this assembly session was to call early elections, and I wanted to show that this wasn't a SDS request but a joint request. But I'm finished with this document and I wish to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: There's not even a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 2D00128, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Which brings us to the ends of today's sitting and we will resume in this courtroom tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 18th day of November, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
